newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - EU to open grain tenders, no hurry to sell.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU to open grain tenders, no hurry to sell.

text.p: A senior EU farm official said on Friday the European Union would launch the keenly awaited mechanism for exporting this year's grain in the next few weeks, but was in no hurry actually to start selling on world markets.

"We will launch the free-market (export) tenders in the coming weeks but we are not pressed (to export)," Jose Manuel Silva, director of cereals and other crops at the European Commission, told reporters at a grain meeting in Paris.

Private traders have for weeks been pressing the EU's executive to open the weekly tender process for exports from the 1997/98 (July/June) harvest, allowing them to bid for subsidies to sell European grain in competition with cheaper U.S. prices.
The EU closed tenders for wheat exports from the previous crop in April, and the deadline for other types of grain expired last week with no new date set for the next campaign to begin.
The Commission effectively controls the pace of exports by accepting or rejecting the bids at each Thursday's tender.
It has recently taken further steps to discourage wheat exports by imposing export taxes through an alternative daily bidding channel until the state of the next crop becomes clear.
Silva said his personal estimate was that this year's harvest would be similar to last year's bumper crop which had given the EU a "positive" export campaign on the world market.
"My view, though it is personal, is that it will be the same picture as last year. But nothing is clear," he said.

That view was echoed by several dealers at the informal grain trading event, who said northern French crops were progressing well after a spring drought, and an increase in area would probably compensate for an expected dip in yields.
Analysts say last year's EU grain harvest was 204 million tonnes, up from just under 180 million in 1995.
Silva said that when regulating exports, the Commission would maintain its basic policy of keeping back enough to put downward pressure on domestic grain prices.
"Our priority is internal consumption and prices. Exporting is important but our priority is the internal market," he said.
He said the EU would continue to track the world market but declined to say whether this meant following the recent softening of U.S. soft red winter to levels below $140 a tonne.
In a speech to grain traders earlier, Silva defended the EU's export performance in the 1996/97 season, saying their criticisms earlier in the year had been unfounded.
He said the EU had broken records in products like flour and malt, and grain sales had also been strong.

"During the whole campaign which has just ended, we conducted a policy whose primary aim was to maintain, and if possible increase, internal grain consumption at affordable prices," Silva said. "We nonetheless succeeded in the exporting the biggest amount of cereals possible, at reasonable world prices and with subsidies which were also very reasonable."
He said the Commission's policy had also been to maximise the exports of high value-added products.

He noted EU-controlled intervention stocks had fallen to two million tonnes from 2.7 million at the start of the season, though stocks were badly distributed. Of the modest total, 86 percent was in Germany, followed by Finland and Ireland.
